title: Otter Attack on Swimmer at Lake Tahoe Mobilizes Authorities
seoTitle: Otter Attack on Swimmer at Lake Tahoe Mobilizes.
subtitle: Swimming instructor needed dozens of stitches after being bitten and scratched by a wild animal.
excerpt: A swimmer was surprised and injured by a river otter in Lake Tahoe, USA, sustaining dozens of cuts.
author: Daniele Morais
sourceName: Los Angeles Times, Tahoe Daily Tribune
contentHtml:
An American river otter attacked a swimming instructor while she was swimming in Lake Tahoe, Nevada, United States. The animal repeatedly bit and scratched the woman, causing injuries to her face, hands, and legs. The unusual case mobilized environmental monitoring teams and drew attention to the presence of these carnivores in the area.

The Attack During the Crossing at Hidden Beach

Swimmer Lynnette Bellin, who works as a children’s swim instructor, was following her usual route along the eastern shore of Lake Tahoe. She entered the water at Hidden Beach, an isolated public beach within Lake Tahoe‑Nevada State Park, heading south toward Sand Harbor. About 30 minutes after she started swimming, Bellin felt something pull at her leg and initially thought it was another person, until she saw the animal lunging with teeth and claws.

The instructor said she tried to push the otter away, but the animal kept delivering bites and scratches to her feet and legs. Bellin noted that her technical familiarity with the water allowed her to focus solely on defending herself, without having to expend energy on breath control or staying afloat.

Escape Over Rocks and Medical Treatment

During the attack, Bellin attempted to climb onto various rocks to get out of the water. Some stones were slippery and caused her to lose balance briefly. The otter retreated only when the swimmer managed to get onto large granite blocks positioned about three meters above the water level.

She then moved past the rocks and a fence to reach the East Shore bike trail. Barefoot and bloodied, Bellin walked roughly 1.2 kilometers back to the beach. The lacerations inflicted by the animal required medical attention and totaled 38 sutures, 22 of which were on her right foot, which swelled.

Search for the Animal and Possible Causes of the Aggression

Nevada’s Department of Wildlife received the alert shortly before 10 a.m. According to the agency’s spokesperson, Kenzie Margiott, agents conducted searches to locate the otter and determine whether it was displaying abnormal behavior, but the mammal was not found.

The agency explained that otter attacks on humans are uncommon and, without examining the specific animal, it is impossible to determine what motivated the aggression. These animals usually avoid contact with people but may act defensively if they feel threatened, cornered, are protecting their young, or defending hunting areas.

Otter Presence and Regional History

River otters are native predators adapted to cold high‑altitude waters and inhabit Lake Tahoe, the Truckee River, and even Pyramid Lake. Members of the weasel family, adult specimens can reach up to 1.2 meters in length and have strong jaws, powerful tails, waterproof fur, and webbed feet.

According to the Tahoe Institute for Natural Science, the species was virtually absent from the basin for decades due to historic trapping, but has been recolonizing the region over the past 15 years. Although rare, attacks have been recorded nearby: in 2023, river otters attacked several people at Serene Lakes near Donner Summit.

With information from Los Angeles Times, Tahoe Daily Tribune.
